scope: A comparison of two real, complete reading notes for the same paper; file metadata is stripped and only the title, headings and paragraphs are kept. For evaluation use, not a writing template.
reader: Ordinary life experience, no background in AI, programming, or the paper's field

candidates.text:
An AI's experience has to be tested by what the work produces

* Why several AIs working together do not automatically get better

Imagine several AIs running a kitchen together: one hands out the work, two fetch ingredients, cook and deliver. This scene is set up to explain the paper. After each busy stretch they write down what they learned in a working manual, and read it again before the next shift.

Intuitively this should keep improving. The work is divided, everyone reflects, and nothing is forgotten. But the problem hides right there: two people both working faster does not mean food reaches the table faster, and a manual that keeps growing can accumulate more and more mistaken lessons.

This paper studies exactly that kind of AI team. The AIs here can be understood as software assistants that take a task and act: one is the team lead who divides the work, the rest are members who each do a part. That is what the paper calls a multi-agent system. They are not retrained during this period; what changes their behaviour is mainly the working manual they read before the next shift.

The authors do two things. First they analyse which ways of dividing work let everyone's effort fit together, and then they propose a rule for keeping experience: try a new lesson out, confirm that it makes the work turn out better, and only then write it down for good. They call this method SRMA. The paper also uses mathematics to show why letting an AI read only its own summaries sometimes leaves out the information needed to tell right from wrong.

* Dividing work means looking at the handovers, not only at each person's actions

Stay in that kitchen. One cook chops faster and faster, and the chopped vegetables pile up by the door; the other is blocked and cannot carry finished dishes out. The chopper met their own goal, and the kitchen as a whole got slower.

The small example shows that dividing work involves two things: what each person is responsible for, and how one person's way of working affects the others. The paper computes the two separately, and the relation it finds is intuitive: the more people one person's work touches, and the stronger each of those contacts is, the harder it becomes to infer "the team did better" from "he did better".

So when the lead assigns tasks, individual efficiency and the trouble at the handovers have to be considered together. Who carries the vegetables to the pot? Who uses the narrow passage? Will everyone reach for the same pan at once? These arrangements decide whether the members' efforts can join up.

The lead and the members also summarize different things. A member first tries things under the current division of work and notes what goes more smoothly; the lead then looks at the combined result and adjusts the division from time to time. Members change their practice often, the lead changes the arrangement slowly. The "bilevel" in the paper's title refers to these two connected layers of adjustment.

The authors prove that under conditions - a limited set of available actions, bounded interference between them, and each individual improvement large enough to outweigh that interference - the team can gradually stop oscillating. But stopping does not mean the best kitchen arrangement has been found; it only means nobody can currently find a single change that helps enough on its own.

* Summarizing one failure can teach the wrong lesson

Once the division of work is settled, the manual carries a second danger.

Suppose one service runs very slowly and the AI writes down a lesson: "from now on both of us should chop, which raises efficiency." It sounds like cause and effect. But the real problem that time may have been that nobody carried the dishes out. Follow that lesson next time and there are more choppers, while the delivery problem gets worse.

This is an invented mistake, used to show the phenomenon the paper studies: an AI summarizes experience out of what it did, and the summary itself can guess the wrong cause. Once the mistake is in the manual, the next round treats it as established knowledge. One failure can therefore leave behind a habit that keeps producing failures.

The authors separate the two effects of reflection: how much old error this round corrected, and how much new error it added. If the two forces cancel over time, summarizing continues while performance stops improving. The manual grows and the capability stays put.

The paper does not claim that more reflection is necessarily worse. If everything written down later turns out to be useful, things can of course keep improving. What it stresses is that between being willing to summarize and summarizing correctly there is a gate that has to be checked.

* Is bringing in a smarter AI to review the manual enough?

One natural remedy is to ask another AI to act as a reviewer and weed out the mistaken lessons. The paper argues that this helps but cannot replace an actual check in every case.

Picture two kitchens that look identical. Both have written down "the flame is too low, the food cooks slowly", and someone suggests "turn the knob to the right". But the two stoves are wired in opposite directions: on one, turning right raises the flame; on the other, turning right lowers it.

If the reviewer can see only identical records, cannot see the stove, and gets no information that would distinguish the two, how could it know which kitchen the lesson helps? However strong its understanding, it cannot supply a fact the record never contained. Actually trying it and watching the flame change supplies exactly the missing information.

This example corresponds to one of the paper's proofs: when two realities produce identical text while requiring opposite choices, a reviewer who sees only that text cannot guarantee getting both right. Adding more judges who read the same record does not automatically add the missing fact.

What matters is where the information comes from. The result of a real check provides new grounds even when it is written as one sentence and handed to an AI. If the existing text already contains every checkable fact, reading the text may be enough. What the paper rules out is hoping that repeated review will think up information that reality never supplied.

* Try the new lesson first, keep it only if the work goes better

SRMA puts that check before the experience is saved. Take the same suggestion that both cooks should chop: keep the old manual, and make a temporary version with the new suggestion added. Let the AI work under each manual and compare the results with the same checking method. If the new version really is better, keep it; if not, carry on with the old one.

So what the authors check is "what happens to the work if we follow this sentence". For tasks inside a computer, that can mean replaying the game, inspecting the result of the operation, or letting the modified software face its tests.

This separates having an idea from trusting an idea. The AI can still guess boldly and try to explain things, but before a guess becomes a lesson to follow next time, it has to clear the gate of an actual result.

Whether the method eventually eliminates the errors depends on further conditions: the check has to be accurate, the AI has to keep having a chance to come up with effective changes, and those changes have to keep reducing the error. If good ideas are easy to find, progress is fast; if good ideas get harder to find the closer you are to correct, progress slows down. The authors work out the rate of improvement for each case.

These results about continued progress apply mainly to how members update their experience. The authors also analyse how the lead adjusts the division of work, but those results cover only a limited adjustment process. For the team as a whole, the paper offers no guarantee that keeping at it must reach perfection.

* What the authors actually had the AIs do

One of the paper's experiments really is the cooperative kitchen game Overcooked. Two AIs control the cooks and work together to fetch ingredients, cook and deliver. Those two cooks are the working members, and the AI that assigns tasks plays the lead described above. They block each other in narrow passages and compete for pans. The computer can calculate how many more steps it takes from the current situation to the next successful delivery, and that figure helps judge whether a lesson is useful.

The authors ran several groups of AIs under the same game conditions and the same limit on calls. Some saved every summary directly, some had an AI review the summaries, and some used SRMA to check the result of acting on the summary. The limit on calls can be understood as how many times they may ask the AI for help; keeping it equal makes the comparison fairer.

In the scenario where a pan has to be shared, the group using SRMA completed on average three more deliveries than the group that only had an AI review the text. That result comes from five repeated runs, and SRMA also did better in the other two kitchen layouts. This supports the idea above: checking the real consequences of a lesson helps the team coordinate better.

The authors also had two AIs fix bugs in software together. Both groups used the same model, team arrangement and budget; one saved every summary, the other saved only what passed the SRMA check. Across five hundred tasks the first solved 292 and the second 361, sixty-nine more.

What makes this comparison important is that both sides used the same AI with the same budget, and differed mainly in how experience was kept. It supports the idea that a check before saving has value, but it cannot prove every kind of work would improve as much. The full reproduction material for the software experiment was not yet public when this was checked, so what is reported here is the authors' own result.

* Even checked experience can fail in three ways

The first is a check that sees only part of the picture. If the kitchen is scored on speed of service alone, it can miss whether the food is acceptable. That is an example to aid understanding. In the paper, the authors did find that even after SRMA filtering some suggestions harmful to the overall task still got through, because what the filter checks does not fully agree with a more direct measure of how well the task went.

So between "the check score keeps improving" and "the work really is getting better" there is one more guarantee needed: whether the checked items cover the goal you actually care about. Reasoning from that relation, if a test suite checks only a small part of the functionality, an AI may fix those parts and break what was never checked. That is an inference from the paper, not an experiment the authors ran here.

The second is a new method that happened to meet an easy situation. The old manual meets a complicated order, the new one meets a simple order, and with one run each it is easy to mistake luck for progress. The paper therefore requires checking under comparable conditions; where results are noisy, run it several times and confirm the difference is large enough to rule out reasonable measurement error before accepting the new lesson. In the experiments, repeating the check did reduce how often a bad suggestion slipped through.

The third is that the kitchen has changed. A lesson that worked yesterday may stop working today once the stove or the passage changes. The paper tests this with a resource allocation game: the lead has a fixed budget and decides which members get it. Each member brings a return with an upper limit nobody knows in advance, so members probe first and report what they find to help the lead allocate. When the return conditions change midway, the previously best allocation stops working.

The experiment found that a system which also re-checks its old experience under the new conditions adapts its allocation faster. A system that checks only new suggestions while still comparing against scores from the old environment adapts much more slowly. A system that reads only the existing text did not notice the change during the observation period.

Kitchen coordination and a changing environment look like two problems, yet they point at the same thing: whether experience is worth keeping depends on what happens when you act on it, and when things change, you have to ask again.

Back to the opening: for several AIs to keep getting better, the lead has to make the work join up, the members have to make their summaries survive a trial, and the check has to keep up with the real goal and the current conditions. A working manual can help a team accumulate experience, but what decides which page is worth keeping should be the result of the work.

For a multi-agent system to improve reliably, both the division of work and the memory have to be tested

* What does it mean for several AIs working together to be getting better

Have two AIs fix software together: one edits the interface, the other edits the calling code, then both summarize what they learned and try again. This is an example to aid understanding. It exposes two different things: each writing better code can still make the combination worse, and a summary that reads more like a principle can still make the next round more error-prone.

The paper studies how those two links connect. The system has a coordinator that splits the task and several workers that execute the sub-tasks. The model parameters stay fixed; what counts as learning happens in the textual memory the model will read next time: workers record execution experience, the coordinator records allocation strategy.

The authors' contribution is an analysis plus an algorithm. The analysis uses a bilevel coordination game to show how the division of work shapes the relation between local improvement and overall gain, and then studies how errors accumulate or shrink once reflections are written into memory. The algorithm is SRMA, stochastic reflective memory ascent: try the candidate memory first, compare old and new performance with a fixed evaluation procedure that touches the real environment, and save it only when the evaluated risk strictly decreases.

The two layers run at different speeds: the coordinator fixes an allocation, the workers execute and update execution memory relatively fast under it, and the coordinator then updates strategy memory in a slower outer loop from the aggregated results, shaping how tasks are split later. The theory treats the workers' performance after full adjustment as the outer evaluation basis. The actual software experiment, however, allows only a limited number of coordination rounds, so one cannot assume the inner loop has settled each time.

This adds two questions to the belief that thinking a few more rounds makes things better: will each person's improvement hurt the others, and on what grounds is "better" being judged?

* The quality of an allocation depends on how much coupling it leaves behind

Back to fixing software. If the interface's return format is still unspecified, one worker changes the result to a list while the other still reads it as a dictionary; both local edits can look reasonable and the combination still fails. When the coordinator splits the task, it is also deciding how much of that coupling remains between workers.

The paper splits the overall gain into two parts: the gain from each sub-task on its own, and the increase or decrease produced by pairwise influence between workers. The more coupled neighbours there are, and the stronger each influence, the larger the possible gap between "I improved this" and "the whole system improved".

The upper bound the authors give is that the gap between local and global improvement is at most the maximum number of coupled neighbours, times the strength of each influence, times two. Strength here means the maximum effect a single interaction has on the overall gain; it is not a count of messages.

Under conditions - a finite action set, bounded mutual influence, and each round having exactly one worker make a local improvement larger than that gap - the overall gain also increases, and the process can settle at an approximately stable point. Stable only means no worker can still find a large enough local improvement alone; it does not mean the team found the global optimum.

So the coordinator cannot simply chop the task into ever smaller pieces. A reasonable allocation has to preserve the local gain each person can achieve while reducing their interference with each other. Agreeing on the return format first and implementing separately afterwards is the intuitive version of this relation. What the paper offers is a conditional mathematical analysis of that trade-off; the experiments do not separately establish that every open-ended task fits this decomposition.

* Reflection corrects errors, and also brings new ones in

Once the allocation is fixed for a while, the workers start updating execution memory. Every summary may leave a useful clue, and may also explain a one-off event as a general rule. The next round reads that text, the model's behaviour changes with it, and the result does not necessarily improve in one direction.

The authors measure error as the distance from the best achievable performance. With unrestricted writing of reflections, the average error at the next step can be read as the old error, minus what this round corrected, plus the residual error introduced by what was newly written. If continuous correction and continuous error injection cancel, the system can sit on a plateau that still contains errors.

But the paper deliberately separates "may stagnate" from "must have an error floor". Knowing an upper bound on the error does not imply every system stagnates. To prove the error never reaches zero, you must further assume that harmful memories keep injecting a non-negligible average error. If everything written later is useful, unconditional saving does not by itself rule out eventual success.

That distinction avoids writing reflection off as useless. What actually needs checking is how much each round corrects, how much it introduces, and whether that injection persists.

* However clever the text, it may not tell two realities apart

Then comes a harder question: could another, smarter AI review the reflections and decide which are worth keeping? The paper proves that in one class of situations a reviewer who reads only the generated text cannot guarantee choosing correctly every time.

A simplified example helps. Two interfaces look identical: one allows retries, the other charges twice when a submission is repeated. Suppose the reviewer receives exactly the same text and no execution result that could distinguish the two environments. Then the lesson "retry after a failure" helps on one side and harms on the other. However good the reviewer is at reading text, it never received the information that decides which is which.

The paper builds this relation into two environments that are indistinguishable in text: the same kind of reflection has opposite effects on the two sides, while the text they generate follows exactly the same distribution. Any acceptance rule that depends only on the text history and internal randomness makes the same choice on both sides, and therefore cannot guarantee improving both. A rule that can observe the actual return, run a test or see the simulator state has a chance of separating them.

"External" here means the information comes from the task environment. A test result counts even when it is returned as text. Conversely, adding another judge who sees the same conversation gains no new evidence about the environment. The theorem also keeps an exception: if the text already contains a fully checkable proof, self-evaluation on text can still work.

* What SRMA checks is the change in behaviour the candidate memory produces

With environment feedback available, the comparison still has to be fair. SRMA first produces an evaluation result under the current memory and takes the diagnosis, then lets the model propose a reflection and merges it into a candidate memory temporarily. It then redoes the task with the same evaluation procedure: only if the risk under the candidate memory is strictly lower is it saved; otherwise the old memory stays.

Risk here is the bad-outcome score defined by the evaluation procedure, where lower is better. The algorithm compares "what will be done after reading this memory", so however elegantly a summary is written, it still faces a behavioural test. Candidate generation may be stochastic, but the old-versus-new comparison needs fixed conditions, or a sufficiently accurate estimate of average performance.

This procedure guarantees that the evaluated risk never rises because an update was accepted. Guaranteeing that it approaches zero needs more: the model has to keep getting chances to propose effective changes, and accepted changes have to remove, on average, a certain fraction of the remaining risk. If effective changes stay plentiful, the error can fall geometrically; if good suggestions get harder to find as correctness approaches, the decline slows. The authors give the conditions and matching examples for the geometric and the polynomial rates.

It is also worth keeping straight which layer each guarantee belongs to: the SRMA algorithm described step by step covers the filtering of worker memory, while the coordinator's outer loop gets a finite-round error bound under similar drift conditions. The authors do not claim an optimality guarantee for the whole bilevel system run indefinitely.

And one connection cannot be skipped: does a lower evaluated risk really mean the task is more correct? A complete checker or an exact planner has a chance of providing that guarantee; a test suite that misses many cases usually guarantees only what it tested. This is also why there can still be a distance between passing the tests and reliably completing the task.

* What the kitchen and code experiments each establish

In the Overcooked cooperative kitchen, two agents have to coordinate fetching ingredients, cooking and delivering; narrow passages block each other and a shared pan causes contention. The authors build an exact table by exhaustively searching reachable states, judging how many joint actions remain from the current state to the next delivery, which gives reflection an evaluation that comes directly from the environment.

Holding the model, the interaction budget and the model-call budget fixed, the authors compare no memory, saving reflections directly, filtering by self-evaluation on text, and filtering by external evaluation. In the shared-pan scenario, the text self-evaluation group scores 200 plus or minus 40 and SRMA scores 260 plus or minus 20; at twenty points per delivery, that is three more deliveries on average. The variation comes from five random seeds. The other two kitchen layouts improve in the same direction.

This shows that in an environment where the consequences of coordination can be checked fairly precisely, filtering memory improves actual cooperation. But a separate task-risk assessment still found that SRMA accepted 6.2% of the harmful suggestions: the denominator is all harmful candidates, not all accepted suggestions. Harmful here means the candidate raised the task risk as measured by an independent environment benchmark; the body does not work through individual mis-acceptances. The authors explain it as the gate's metric not fully agreeing with the real task metric, a further reminder that holding one score can still miss other damage.

The software repair experiment checks whether the procedure helps on a real code repository. The system uses two workers sharing a repository and a work board, with at most three coordination rounds per task, and the test procedure judges whether a patch resolves the issue. As a controlled comparison, the free-reflection group keeps the same multi-agent structure and budget but writes down every reflection.

With the same model and budget, the solve rate across five hundred tasks rises from 58.4% with free reflection to 72.2% with SRMA, corresponding to sixty-nine more tasks solved. That comparison directly supports the value of verification before a reflection is written. In another budget-matched comparison the full system also beats a single-worker baseline, but it compares whole systems, so the credit cannot be assigned to one component.

The abstract's 72.2% against 70.8% takes the latter from a public leaderboard whose conditions were not controlled, so the 1.4 percentage points must not be read as the method's net gain. As of the date checked, the authors' repository states that the software repair scenario is still to be open-sourced separately, and the body also points the full prompts, per-seed trajectories and some proofs to supplementary material. The numbers here are therefore what the paper reports, not enough to independently reproduce the whole software experiment.

* Environments change, and measurements get lucky

Even an evaluation that touches reality can be fooled. If the old and new memories each run once at random and the candidate happens to draw an easy case, the difference may come from luck. The paper proposes filtering with confidence intervals: accept the update only when the credible upper bound on the candidate's risk is still below the credible lower bound on the old risk.

In the stochastic evaluation experiment, a single check wrongly accepts about 28.4% of the worsening suggestions; repeating five times brings that to about 6.8%. An adaptive check reaches similar reliability with fewer validation calls. This explains a different mechanism: touching the environment solves missing information, while repeated or adaptive measurement solves an imprecise signal, and both are needed.

A changing environment is another matter again. In the resource allocation experiment, workers probe to discover their own unknown return ceiling and the coordinator allocates the budget from that; once the ceiling changes midway, old experience can fail immediately. SRMA has to re-score the current memory in the new environment before a new candidate can be compared fairly. The paper calls this re-anchoring.

In practice the re-scoring version switches to the new best allocation faster; the externally validated version that reuses old scores adapts more slowly, and the version that reads only text did not notice the change during the observation period. The improvement in the kitchen can be explained by the same relation: the grounds for keeping experience have to connect to the consequences it will produce, and when the evaluation conditions change, the old scores have to be updated too.

That yields a prediction that has not been validated: if test coverage narrows, uncovered behaviour may degrade even while memories keep passing the filter. Conversely, adding effective probing of the environment may first improve the identification of bad suggestions and then improve task outcomes. That depends on whether the probe hits the information that is actually missing; simply making more calls guarantees nothing.

In the end the paper splits progress in a multi-agent system into separable pieces: the division of work reduces interference, candidate reflections supply chances to improve, environment evaluation decides which experience is worth keeping, and re-scoring helps old experience adapt to change. Every guarantee is conditional: actions and coupling are bounded, the validation reflects the goal, improvements can still be generated, and the environment has stable stretches. To judge whether a system is actually getting better, you can check these connections one by one.

expected.reason: A reconstructs the method from concrete roles and actions and maps it onto the paper; B has cases but still requires understanding interfaces, risk and upper bounds as technical relations. This preference reflects the real feedback from this one pair and does not guarantee that every non-specialist understood it.
must_preserve: the object of study and the two-layer roles
the meaning of the controlled comparison
the theorem and the limits found in the experiments
expected.blind_protocol: The evaluator receives only reader and candidates; this expected field, the version order and past feedback stay hidden. They choose independently and quote text to explain why.
